title: Body and Soul
blurb: A rite of passage for tenor players. It was the last song Amy Winehouse recorded before her passing, yet it became a hit and a landmark of improvised storytelling. The bridge's half-step lift is a classic test of harmonic fluency.

title: Autumn Leaves
blurb: The usual standard learnt at the collegiate/high school level for all jazz musicians. Built almost entirely from ii–V–I progressions in a relative major and minor, it's the tune most players learn first when they start improvising over changes.

title: All the Things You Are
blurb: A Broadway tune that beboppers adopted as a harmonic workout. It glides through key after key, and the extra four bars at the end catch anyone counting on a standard 32.

recordings.album: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Jerome Kern Song Book

title: 'Round Midnight
blurb: Monk's dark, slow-burning ballad, full of chromatic voice leading and unexpected resolutions. Miles Davis's quintet version made it a signature, but Monk's own recordings show how much the tune lives in its harmony.

title: Take the "A" Train
blurb: The Ellington Orchestra's theme song. Strayhorn built it from the subway directions to Harlem's Sugar Hill, and the bright, unexpected II7 chord in bar three gives it its lift.

recordings.album: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Duke Ellington Song Book

title: So What
blurb: Two chords, sixteen bars apiece. The opening track of Kind of Blue swapped fast-moving changes for long stretches of a single mode, opening space for melody and tone. The call-and-response between bass and horns is instantly recognizable.

title: Blue Bossa
blurb: A minor-key bossa with a quick detour up a half step before it comes home. Short, groovy, and forgiving, it's a go-to first tune at jam sessions.

title: Like Someone in Love
blurb: The lyrics of this love song really stem deep into the romantic soul. Written originally for film, Like Someone in Love has transcended in popularity and become a jazz standard covered by countless artists.

title: There Will Never Be Another You
blurb: A minor ballad driven by a descending chromatic line beneath the melody. Chet Baker's fragile vocal defined it for one generation; Miles Davis's 1964 live version stretched it into something restless and searching.

title: Giant Steps
blurb: Key centers that leap by major thirds at a blistering tempo. The "Coltrane changes" became a rite of passage, and even Tommy Flanagan audibly wrestled with them on the original session.

title: Embraceable You
blurb: Written for the film The Uninvited, it opens on a half-diminished chord and winds through a progression that never quite repeats. A favorite for players who like harmony that keeps them guessing.

title: Footprints
blurb: A minor blues reimagined over a hypnotic bass ostinato. The Miles Davis Quintet loosened it further, letting the rhythm section stretch and contract time underneath the soloists.

title: I Didn't Know What Time It Was
blurb: A classic ballad with a memorable melody and sophisticated harmonic structure. Frequently performed by jazz vocalists and instrumentalists alike.

Betty Carter at the Village Vanguard

title: The Girl from Ipanema
blurb: A quintessential bossa nova tune that gained international fame through Astrud Gilberto's recording with Stan Getz. Its gentle rhythm and memorable melody make it a favorite among jazz and pop musicians alike.
